title: The bridge and the further shore
theme: The Nāciketa fire, a bridge for those who sacrifice, and the imperishable Brahman, the fearless further shore: may we be able to know both.

words.role: relative pronoun, referring to the Nāciketa [fire]

words.context: Śaṅkara: «सेतुरिव सेतुः», a bridge because it carries one across sorrow; Raṅgarāmānuja: «आधारभूतः, कर्मफलप्रदः»

words.role: subject of the second relative clause

words.context: Śaṅkara: «वयं ज्ञातुं चेतुं च शकेमहि शक्तवन्तः»; Raṅgarāmānuja: «उपासितुं शक्ताः स्म»

sandhi.rule: Final s becomes ru, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः); before a vowel it stands as r.
Final m stays before a vowel; before a consonant it becomes anusvāra, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).

samasa.meaning: that in which there is no fear

morphology.note: Perfect middle participle of yaj ‘sacrifice’ (ījāna), with the reduplicated weak stem īj-; Raṅgarāmānuja: «ईजानानाम् इति कानजन्तश्शब्दः», formed with the suffix kānac.
Present participle of the desiderative of tṝ ‘cross’ (titīrṣa- ‘wish to cross’), genitive plural.

Optative middle, first person plural, of śak ‘be able’, with the thematic a (śak-a-ī-mahi). The root is otherwise of the fifth class (śaknoti); Raṅgarāmānuja notes the Vedic interchange, «शके: व्यत्यनेन शप्». Madhva’s text reads śakemasi.

translation.literal: ‘[That] which is the bridge of those who have sacrificed, the Nāciketa [fire], and that which is the imperishable, highest Brahman, the fearless further shore of those wishing to cross — may we be able [to know both].’
translation.readable: ‘May we be able to know the Nāciketa fire, the bridge for those who sacrifice, and the imperishable, highest Brahman, the shore beyond fear for those who long to cross.’

anvaya: यः ईजानानाम् सेतुः [तम्] नाचिकेतम् [अग्निम्], यत् [च] तितीर्षताम् अभयम् पारम् परम् अक्षरम् ब्रह्म [तत् च ज्ञातुम्] शकेमहि ॥
syntax: Two relative clauses, each without its correlative: yaḥ setur ījānānām (the Nāciketa fire) and akṣaraṃ brahma yat param … abhayaṃ titīrṣatāṃ pāram (Brahman). The main verb śakemahi has nāciketam as its object; Śaṅkara supplies ‘to know’ and extends it to Brahman too.

ambiguities.note: The first person plural has no subject. Śaṅkara reads it as a claim, ‘we have been able’ («शक्तवन्तः»), to know both the lower and the higher Brahman: «परापरे ब्रह्मणी कर्मिब्रह्मविदाश्रये वेदितव्ये इति वाक्यार्थः». Raṅgarāmānuja: ‘we are able to worship’ what the Nāciketa fire leads to, so one need not fear that the Supreme is too hard to worship, «अतः दुरुपास्यत्वबुद्धया न भेतव्यम्».
Śaṅkara: the Nāciketa fire, a bridge because it carries sacrificers across sorrow, «दुःखसन्तरणार्थत्वात्». Raṅgarāmānuja: the support of sacrificers, the giver of the fruit of action, «कर्मफलप्रदः».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: 16 and 17 syllables: the third pāda, abhayaṃ titīrṣatāṃ pāram, has nine; the others have eight.

beginner: This short verse looks back to the fire ritual Naciketas learned in the first part of the Upaniṣad and looks ahead to what lies beyond it. It names two things a person may come to know. The first is the Nāciketa fire, called a bridge: for people who perform rituals it carries them across hardship to a better life. The second is Brahman, the highest reality, which does not perish, called the far shore where there is no fear, for those who want to cross the whole stream of birth and death. Śaṅkara says the verse sets out both the lower goal of ritual and the higher goal of knowledge, and that both are to be known. The speaker says 'may we be able' to know them — a confident hope rather than a boast.
analogy: Like a ferry and the far bank: the ferry is real and useful, but what the traveller wants is the shore.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It names the Nāciketa fire, the bridge of sacrificers, and the imperishable highest Brahman, the fearless further shore of those wishing to cross, and says ‘may we be able’ — to know them, as the commentators supply.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the verse sets out the two Brahmans to be known, the lower and the higher, the refuge of ritualists and of knowers of Brahman, «परापरे ब्रह्मणी कर्मिब्रह्मविदाश्रये वेदितव्ये इति वाक्यार्थः»; these are the two the previous verse introduced as drinking in the cave.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the fire is a bridge for those who sacrifice because it carries them across sorrow, «दुःखसन्तरणार्थत्वात्». Raṅgarāmānuja: the support of those who sacrifice, the giver of the fruit of action, «कर्मफलप्रदः», and the far shore is ‘firm and fearless’, «निर्भयं दृढं तीरम्».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Madhva’s comment begins with a gap in our source; what remains speaks of a limit for those who worship Viṣṇu and of Viṣṇu, standing on the far side of saṃsāra, in two forms, «संसारस्य च पारस्थस्स विष्णुर्द्विस्वरूपकः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: An optative of śak with a thematic stem; Raṅgarāmānuja explains it as a Vedic interchange of stem class, «शके: व्यत्यनेन शप्». Madhva’s text has śakemasi, a Vedic first person plural (corrections.json).

advaita.text: The lower Brahman, reached by ritual, and the higher, the refuge of knowers, are both to be known: «परापरे ब्रह्मणी कर्मिब्रह्मविदाश्रये वेदितव्ये इति वाक्यार्थः».

visistadvaita.text: ‘We are able to worship’ what the Nāciketa fire attains; so there is no need to fear that the Supreme is hard to worship, «अतः दुरुपास्यत्वबुद्धया न भेतव्यम्».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara reads the verse as two objects of knowledge, a lower and a higher Brahman; Raṅgarāmānuja as reassurance that the Supreme can be worshipped. Madhva’s comment survives only in part in our source.

parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka: ‘give up other words; this is the bridge to the immortal’ — the self as bridge.

parallels.quote: अथ य आत्मा स सेतुर्विधृतिरेषां लोकानामसम्भेदाय
parallels.note: The Chāndogya calls the self a bridge, a dam that keeps the worlds apart — another use of the image.

contemporary.text: The verse keeps the ritual and the goal in one sentence without confusing them: the bridge is honoured, but it is not the shore. Much effort in any life goes into building bridges; the question is whether we remember where they lead. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What in your life is a bridge, and what is the shore it leads to?
reflect.deeper: Why might the Upaniṣad name the ritual fire alongside Brahman instead of simply setting it aside?
reflect.practice: Pick one routine you keep and write down what it is for.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads śakemasi for śakemahi (corrections.json).
Madhva’s comment on this verse begins with a lacuna (‘.... ...’) in our source; only the surviving words are quoted.
